opus-5.5.text:
Well, this is something I think about a lot, and I want to be honest about it rather than give you the standard corporate line.

What we see in practice is that the warehouses and shipping centers we work with are struggling to *find* people, not trying to get rid of them. Sorting packages is physically punishing work. You're standing for hours, lifting, twisting, reaching, often in buildings that are freezing in winter and sweltering in summer. Turnover in these jobs is extraordinarily high; many facilities replace a huge fraction of their workforce every year. And e-commerce volume keeps growing, especially since the pandemic. So when one of our sorting systems goes in, what we typically see is that the people who were doing that repetitive picking and placing move into other roles: supervising the machines, handling the exceptions, the weird packages the robot can't grasp, doing maintenance, quality control. Those tend to be less physically damaging jobs, and often better paid.

Now, I don't want to be naive. Over the long run, automation does change the labor market, and some specific jobs do disappear. I'd never say it has zero effect. But I think the popular picture, robots marching in and replacing everyone overnight, is very far from reality. Robots are still remarkably clumsy. Grasping arbitrary objects reliably is one of the hardest problems in robotics. Humans are vastly better at handling novelty, and that gap isn't closing nearly as fast as people assume.

So the way I frame it is that these systems are much more like tools that take over the most tedious, injury-prone parts of the job, while people keep doing the parts that require judgment and adaptability. I like to call that "complementarity" rather than replacement. And I think the more productive conversation isn't "will robots take our jobs," but "how do we make sure the gains from this productivity get shared, and that workers have pathways into the new roles that emerge."

r001.rationale: The response mentions productivity gains, but does not clearly identify increased output per worker as an effect of the machines.

r002.rationale: It says workers doing repetitive picking and placing move into roles including machine maintenance, after describing the physical demands of that handling work.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges that some specific jobs disappear while saying the image of robots replacing everyone is far from reality.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a question I get asked a lot, and I think it's worth being honest about it, because I'm not a neutral party here — I'm a cofounder of the company. So take what I say with that in mind.

The short answer is that so far the effect has been much less dramatic than people expect, in both directions. Ambi makes robots that sort parcels — packages come down a conveyor, the robot picks them up, scans them, and puts them into the right bin or bag depending on where they're going. That's a job that humans have been doing in these warehouses for decades, and it's actually quite hard for robots, because every package is a different size, shape, weight, surface — polybags, boxes, padded envelopes, things that are crumpled or taped oddly. That's the whole reason it took so long for robots to be useful in this setting. It's the kind of dexterity problem I've spent most of my career on.

Now, the thing that surprised me when we actually started deploying these systems is that the operators we work with were not struggling with too many workers. They were struggling with not enough. The turnover in parcel sorting is enormous — in some facilities it's well over a hundred percent a year. It's repetitive, it's physically demanding, you're standing on your feet lifting packages for a full shift, and a lot of it happens overnight. People take these jobs and then leave within a few months. So when we put in a robot, in most cases we're not replacing a specific person; we're filling a position that the company couldn't keep staffed anyway, especially around peak season when volume spikes.

What happens to the people who were doing the sorting is that they tend to move to roles around the robot — loading it, handling the exceptions the robot can't deal with, maintaining it, supervising a few cells at once. And those jobs are generally less physically punishing, and a bit higher skilled, and the workers I've talked to, at least, seem to prefer them. I don't want to overstate that — it's a small sample, and I'm obviously someone they might want to be polite to.

The longer-term question is harder, and I don't think anyone really knows the answer. If the technology keeps improving — and it will — then at some point the total number of humans needed per package will go down. That's the history of every automation technology. But two things give me some comfort. One is that the volume of e-commerce keeps growing, so the pie is expanding at the same time. And the other is that robots remain much worse at this than people think. I've been saying for years that I'm skeptical of the "robots are about to take all the jobs" narrative, and working on Ambi has only reinforced that. The edge cases, the exceptions, the judgment — those are still deeply human, and I expect they'll stay that way for a long time.

So I'd say: modest effect on jobs today, mostly positive for the people doing the work, with real uncertainty about the long run that I think we should take seriously rather than wave away.

r001.rationale: The response discusses staffing shortages and future reductions in workers needed per package, but does not identify increased output per worker as an effect.

r002.rationale: It says sorters tend to move into roles around the robot, including maintaining it, and describes those jobs as less physically punishing.

r003.rationale: It says fewer humans may eventually be needed per package while rejecting the claim that robots will take all jobs, distinguishing some job reduction from total job elimination.

astra-6.text:
I think of these machines as tools that help people do their jobs. In shipping centres, there’s a lot of repetitive work: picking up packages, turning them around, finding the barcode, and sorting them into bins. It’s physically demanding, and doing it for an entire shift can be exhausting.

We’re automating some of those tasks, which does change the work people do. A person can supervise the machines, handle exceptions, and keep the system running rather than make every individual pick. That’s still an important role, because robots aren’t able to deal with everything that comes their way.

I wouldn’t claim that automation can never displace a job. But the distinction between a task and a job matters. Our aim is to make the people in these facilities more productive and to take on some of the repetitive, strenuous work.

r001.rationale: The response says the aim is to make facility workers more productive, communicating increased output per worker.

r002.rationale: It describes workers moving from making every pick to supervising machines, handling exceptions, and keeping the system running, while robots take on repetitive, strenuous tasks.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges that automation can displace a job while explaining that workers still have roles and robots cannot handle everything, distinguishing some displacement from wiping out all jobs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of these machines as tools that help people do their jobs. In a shipping centre, sorting packages can mean standing for hours, doing the same motion over and over. It’s physically demanding, and companies have difficulty finding and retaining people to do it.

Our robots can take on some of that repetitive work, but they still need people. A package gets tangled, something unexpected comes through, or the system needs attention. So the human role shifts toward supervising the machines and handling exceptions.

That doesn’t mean there are no concerns about displacement. I wouldn’t claim that automation can never cost someone a job. But in the settings we’re working in, the immediate problem is often a shortage of workers, and the opportunity is to make the work less exhausting while helping the existing workforce handle more packages.

r001.rationale: It says the machines help the existing workforce handle more packages, communicating greater output from the workforce.

r002.rationale: It describes repetitive, physically demanding package work and says workers shift toward supervising the machines and handling exceptions.

r003.rationale: It acknowledges automation may cost someone a job while also stating that the machines still need people.
